citation.title: Changes in interest group access in times of crisis: no pain, no (lobby) gain
citation.venue_or_publisher: Journal of European Public Policy, 29(9), 1374-1394 (published online 30 Aug 2021)
citation.type: publisher's version (Taylor & Francis open access PDF; page 2 says it was republished with minor changes that do not affect the academic content)

question: Whether organisations whose interests were most affected by the Covid-19 outbreak gained more access to government, parliament, the bureaucracy and the media, and whether this differs for economic and non-economic interests.
data: Online elite survey of interest group and large firm leaders in ten European polities (Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden, UK, EU level), early June to mid-July 2020; sample of over 7,000 organisations, 1441 complete responses (response rate 20.4 per cent, 7 to 42 per cent by country). Organisations drawn as stratified samples from lobbying registers and scholars' population lists.
method: Respondents rated their access frequency (never to almost daily) to four venues before and during the crisis; the change is the difference. Main predictor is self-rated affectedness (1 to 5, relative to other stakeholders). OLS regressions with country fixed effects and standard errors clustered by sector; controls for organisation type, lobbying staff and age; interactions tested. Robustness checks (ordered logit, alternative sector-based affectedness measure) are in appendices that are not in this file. Organisation type is taken from the respondent's own classification. No language model and no coder agreement are used.

definitions.definition: Quoted from Binderkrantz and Pedersen (2017): a group has entered a political arena by passing a threshold controlled by gatekeepers. The authors treat access as a two-way process of seeking and granting.
definitions.quote: a group has entered a political arena (parliament, administration, or media) passing a threshold controlled by relevant gatekeepers (politicians, civil servants, or journalists)

definitions.definition: How strongly an organisation's interests are hit by an external shock; a dynamic characteristic of interest organisations.
definitions.quote: We here understand aﬀectedness as a central dynamic characteristic of interest organizations when they face external challenges or threats

definitions.definition: One of three types, taken from respondents' own classification: business associations and firms are grouped together as one category.
definitions.quote: where respondents classiﬁed the type of organization, we distinguish three categories: 1) business organizations, including business associations and ﬁrms; 2) profession groups, including professional

definitions.definition: The non-economic category: cause-centred groups, NGOs and citizen associations.
definitions.quote: public interest groups, which contains cause-centered groups, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and citizen associations

definitions.definition: Economic interests are business organisations plus profession groups (professional associations and labour unions); non-economic are public interest groups.
definitions.quote: organizations representing economic interests (i.e., business organizations and professional groups), and non-economic interests, (i.e., public interest groups)

proxies.indicator: Respondent's self-rating on a 1 to 5 scale compared with other stakeholders in the country.
proxies.quote: on a scale ranging from 1 (much less aﬀected) to 5 (much more aﬀected)

proxies.indicator: The authors' own categorisation of sectors as less or more highly affected; details are in Appendix D, not in this file. The sector scheme itself is not described in the main text.
proxies.quote: our own categorization of less and more highly aﬀected sectors

proxies.indicator: Number of full-time staff in public affairs, grouped into three categories.
proxies.quote: low (<1), medium (1–4) and high (>=5) lobbying staﬀresources

proxies.indicator: Stratified samples from lobbying registers and scholars' lists, to give similar total samples per country and similar shares of organisation types.
proxies.quote: The stratiﬁed samples were drawn to ensure the inclusion of 1) similar total samples across countries, and 2) similar shares of diﬀerent types of organizations in each polity.

findings.claim: Affectedness predicts increases in access to all four venues (media, government, parliament, bureaucracy).
findings.quote: organizations that saw their interests more aﬀected during this crisis increased their access more than less aﬀected groups

findings.claim: Business organisations gained more access than public interest groups, mainly in media and parliament.
findings.quote: it is mainly in the media and parliamentary arena that business access has increased signiﬁcantly more

findings.claim: Affected public interest groups did not gain as much access as affected business, labour or professional groups.
findings.quote: highly aﬀected public interest groups, which usually represent social or environmental causes, were not able to increase their access as much as aﬀected business organizations

findings.claim: Public interest groups were not predicted to increase access in any venue, even when highly affected.
findings.quote: In none of the venues, even at the highest level of aﬀectedness, are public interest groups predicted to have increased their access.

limitations.point: Affectedness is self-rated and relative, so it may be over- or under-estimated.
limitations.quote: a downside is that this rating is subject to potential over- or under estimation and requires an implicit comparison to other stakeholders in a given country

limitations.point: Very low response rates in some countries.
limitations.quote: For Italy, France, and the UK we register very low response rates between ca. 13 per cent (Italy) and 7 per cent (UK).
Importantly, our analysis focused on short-term changes in access.

limitations.point: Appendices (sampling frame, sector scheme, robustness tables) are not in the extracted file, so the sector coding cannot be checked. The article has no climate, UN or fossil fuel content.
